infra-context

Infra map: Validate Multitenant

How the system is built, run and deployed, and the budgets it must hold. Source paths are relative to the two sibling repositories: BE = ms_validate_tenant_backend, FE = spa_validate_tenant_frontend, both on branch sbx. This map holds the architecture, external-service and non-functional sections; the backend, frontend, environment and CI/CD sections were added by Phase 3.

Overview

Pattern. A single-page admin application talks to one ASP.NET Core API built as Clean Architecture (API, Application, Domain, Infrastructure projects). Every request crosses an nginx reverse proxy that terminates TLS. The API keeps its business data in PostgreSQL, uses Redis for tenant-keyed cache entries, MongoDB for operational and technical logs, and RabbitMQ to hand ATDP download requests to an external worker. The pattern is a monolithic API with a separate static front end, not microservices: the repository name says "ms" but the code is one deployable (BE/MultitenantValidate.sln).

Deployment shape. Development and QA run as one Docker Compose project of seven containers (nginx, front end, API, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, RabbitMQ) on a private bridge network, with nginx publishing the web ports (18080 and 18443), and PostgreSQL additionally bound to host loopback port 15432. Production runs the same services on the client's Kubernetes cluster according to BE/docs/Despliegue.md; no Kubernetes manifests exist in either repository (see discovery-gaps). The backend, frontend, environment and CI/CD detail is Phase 3's.

Containers and data flow

Everything the figure shows, in words: the browser loads the Angular build from the front-end container through nginx on port 18443, then sends all /api/ calls through the same nginx to the API container on port 8080 (a separate /api/sse/ location keeps a long-lived stream open, with a 3600-second read timeout). The API reads and writes PostgreSQL through EF Core; calls Redis for the tenant cache and its health check; writes business-operation logs and Serilog entries to MongoDB; publishes ATDP export requests to RabbitMQ (exchange atdp.download.main); sends activation e-mails through an SMTP server; and calls the ATDP worker over HTTP to fetch a PDF. The worker that consumes the queue and the biometric components that call the machine routes live outside these repositories. The current working-tree Compose file additionally binds PostgreSQL's container port 5432 to host loopback at 127.0.0.1:15432 for local access; this bypasses nginx.

Auth flow

  1. On application start the SPA generates an ephemeral ECDH P-256 key pair and posts its public key to POST /api/handshake (anonymous).
  2. The API creates its own ephemeral key pair, derives a 32-byte AES-GCM key with HKDF-SHA256 (salt and info are literals shared by both code bases), stores it in process memory under a new session id (30 minutes sliding, 8 hours at most), and answers with the session id and its public key. Both sides now hold the same key.
  3. The user logs in at POST /api/auth/login/admin or /login/tenant with the body encrypted as {ct, nonce} and the headers X-Session-Id and X-Timestamp (accepted within 60 seconds; a nonce is accepted once, for two minutes).
  4. On success the API sets three cookies: access_token (JWT, 15 minutes) and refresh_token (7 days, path /api), both HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite=Strict, plus a readable csrf_token. The refresh token is stored hashed and rotated. In Production the tokens are blanked in the response body; outside Production they are also returned there.
  5. Every mutating call then carries the cookies, the X-CSRF-Token header (must equal the cookie) and an encrypted body; GET calls send only X-Session-Id and receive an encrypted response. A 401 triggers a single shared refresh through POST /api/auth/refresh.
  6. Machine clients skip the envelope: POST /api/auth/login/api exchanges a tenant client id and secret for a bearer token, used on /api/Synchronize/*. Twelve route prefixes require encryption (tenant, branch, terminal, device, userrapp, auth, operator, user, role, product, logs, contingency); multipart uploads are sent unencrypted.

Request pipeline order in Program.cs: error handler, security headers, auth-response middleware, Swagger (non-Production), seeder, CORS, HSTS and HTTPS redirect (non-Development), rate limiter, payload decryption, synchronize-bearer translation, JWT authentication, CSRF check, single-use API token check, authorization, health endpoint, controllers.

Database at architecture level

PostgreSQL 16 holds all business entities and is reached through EF Core repositories (one per aggregate, soft delete and an audit-log table). The provider is chosen by the DatabaseProvider setting: Postgres (default) or SQL Server, with separate connection strings; only the PostgreSQL path was seen running. Migrations are code-first (31 files in BE/MultitenantValidate.Infrastructure/Infrastructure/Migrations) and are applied automatically at API start by the seeder (DataBaseSeeder.cs), which also creates the first administrator; a seeder failure is logged and the API keeps running. MongoDB stores two databases (operational "NR" logs and Serilog entries); Redis holds tenant-keyed cache entries; RabbitMQ carries ATDP export messages. Entities, columns, relationships and state machines are in business-data-context, not here.

Security architecture

Authentication: JWT bearer (cookie or header) with four principal types in a user-type claim (Admin, TenantAdmin, UserApp, TenantApi); authorization by named policies built on that claim plus a tenant-access filter. Data protection: TLS 1.3 at nginx and Kestrel with HSTS (one year, preload), application-layer AES-GCM on API payloads, BCrypt password hashes, AES-GCM encryption of stored secrets under a master key, five-entry credential history. Defences: per-address rate limits, failed-login blocking, user lockout, CSRF double-submit, replay protection (nonce and timestamp), response headers including a strict API content security policy. Detail and evidence per control: nfr-security.

Performance hooks

Redis keys of the form client:<rnec>, user:<rnec>:<username>, branch:, bm: and tx: are invalidated by the API after writes (TenantCacheService.cs); the code that fills them was not found in these repositories. Sliding-window rate limits protect authentication routes. Static front-end assets are served with one-year immutable caching. Detail: nfr-performance.

nginx role

nginx is the only published web entry point; PostgreSQL is separately bound to host loopback at 127.0.0.1:15432. nginx redirects port 80 to HTTPS, enforces TLS 1.3, adds HSTS, proxies /api/ (60-second timeouts) and /api/sse/ (unbuffered, 3600-second read timeout) to the API and the rest to the front-end container, which has its own nginx with a content security policy. It sets X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto, but no forwarded-headers handling was found in the API (see discovery-gaps).

Architecture decisions

ADR-0018 (Proposed, discovered): tests authenticate through the real encrypted session instead of the non-production plaintext fallback. Nobody decided it in this session; it records what the code forces and one open question.

QA relevance

  • Components to test: the API (105 operations in the live Swagger), the SPA flows per role, the machine routes (Synchronize, Validation), the ATDP export chain (API, queue, external worker).
  • Automation is harder than usual for four reasons: bodies and responses are encrypted on the wire for twelve route prefixes, so a plain HTTP client cannot read or write them without a crypto helper; mutating calls need a CSRF token read from a cookie; login is limited to four failed attempts per 30 seconds per address and users can lock out; and the OpenAPI document describes plaintext shapes while the wire carries {ct, nonce}.
  • Behaviour depends on the environment name: outside Production the API accepts plaintext bodies when no session id is sent, skips the CSRF check in Development when the header is absent, exposes Swagger, and returns tokens in the login body. A Production-like environment is needed to test the real contract.
  • Environment requirements: PostgreSQL, Redis, MongoDB and RabbitMQ all healthy (/api/health checks four of them), a reachable SMTP server for tenant-admin activation e-mails, and the ATDP worker for the download flow.

ATDP worker. Its failure maps to a 503-class business error ("service not available", codes for not configured and unavailable); a missing record is answered with HTTP 422 by the worker and handled. Tests of the download flow need a stub or the real worker, and the queue consumer is not in these repositories.

SMTP. If the server is unreachable the activation e-mail is not delivered; a test that needs the activation link must read the mailbox or use a catch-all test server (the example configuration names Mailtrap for development).

Redis. Only invalidation was found in the API, so entries must be created by another component (probably the validation service outside these repositories); with Redis unset the API silently uses memory.

With more than one API replica, a crypto session created on one replica is unknown to the others and a request routed to another replica returns the "crypto session expired" error, unless the ingress uses sticky sessions. Whether the client's cluster does this was not verifiable. QA relevance: any test environment with more than one API instance must be checked for this first.

Build-time versus run-time: nothing is read at build time; the Dockerfile only restores and publishes. Configuration is loaded in this order: appsettings.json (required, optional: false), appsettings.<ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT>.json (optional), then environment variables, which win.

Local development recipe

Two ways to run the API. The Compose route is the one that reproduces the QA stack and the one the framework targets (https://localhost:18443).

# A. Full stack with Docker Compose (nginx, API, SPA, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, RabbitMQ)
# Both repositories must be sibling folders (compose builds ../spa_validate_tenant_frontend)
cd ms_validate_tenant_backend
cp .env.example .env
# Edit .env: type the secret values yourself (JWT_KEY, MASTER_KEY, SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD, RABBITMQ_PASSWORD, EMAIL_*).
# For Swagger and plaintext fallback set ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT to a non-Production value (default is Production).
# TLS: nginx needs nginx/certs/fullchain.pem and nginx/certs/privkey.pem (git-ignored; any localhost certificate works)
docker compose up -d --build
curl -sk https://localhost:18443/api/health

# B. API only, on the host (needs PostgreSQL, Redis, MongoDB and RabbitMQ reachable)
# Requires MultitenantValidate.API/appsettings.json, which is git-ignored and has no template (see discovery-gaps)
dotnet run --project MultitenantValidate.API --launch-profile https
curl -sk https://localhost:7096/api/health

Health check: GET /api/health returns {status, checks[]} with the checks redis, postgres, mongodb and rabbitmq. Read on the running local stack on 2026-10-23: all four Healthy.

Auth flow: the real login requests

The sequence, cookies, envelope rules, CSRF and the twelve encrypted route prefixes are in architecture (Auth flow); not repeated here. What the test framework needs, request by request:

StepRequestBody and headersWhat comes back
1. HandshakePOST /api/handshake (anonymous, never encrypted){ "clientPublicKey": "<base64 SPKI of an ephemeral P-256 key>" }Envelope in PascalCase: { Ok, Data: { SessionId, ServerPublicKey } } (base64 SPKI). The SPA derives the AES-GCM key from both keys
2. Administrator loginPOST /api/auth/login/adminPlain shape { userName, password } (LoginDto), sent as { ct, nonce } (base64 ciphertext plus tag, 12-byte nonce); headers X-Session-Id, X-TimestampEncrypted BaseResponse; cookies access_token, refresh_token (HttpOnly) and csrf_token (readable)
2b. Tenant loginPOST /api/auth/login/tenantSame shape and headers as step 2Same cookies
3. Mutating callany POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE under /apiCookies, header X-CSRF-Token equal to the csrf_token cookie, encrypted body, X-Session-IdEncrypted response
4. RefreshPOST /api/auth/refreshCookies (the SPA sends an empty body)New cookies; refresh token is rotated
5. LogoutPOST /api/auth/logoutCookiesCookies cleared, tokens revoked
Machine loginPOST /api/auth/login/apiHeaders ClientId and ClientSecret; body { "data": "<string>" } (ApiLoginRequestDto; the inner shape ApiLoginInnerDto is { UserName, Password })Bearer token for /api/Synchronize/*. How data is encoded is shown by generate-api-login-payload.js and was not read

Outside Production the login response body also carries the tokens, and a request without X-Session-Id is accepted in plaintext. Login is limited to four failures per 30 seconds per address. Credentials: by variable name only; the framework names for the SUT users are LOCAL_USER_EMAIL and LOCAL_USER_PASSWORD in this repository's .env.example (values never recorded). Contract decision: ADR-0018.

The SUT's /qa page. Not present: the local stack answers GET /qa with the SPA shell (the Angular fallback), which has no data-testid="qa-page" root. Optional input, not a gap.

Routing, state and auth integration points

  • Routes (app.routes.ts): public /login, /change-password, /activate; inside the shell (guarded by authGuard): /dashboard, /tenants, /users, /operators, /settings, /products, /log-consultas-nr, /log-peticiones-nr, /log-respuestas-no-satisfactorias-nr (administrators), the three /logs/... twins (tenant users) and /admin-panel (tenant super administrator). Unknown paths redirect to /, which redirects by role: tenant super admin to /admin-panel, user application to /logs/consultas-nr, everyone else to /dashboard.
  • Guards: authGuard, adminGuard, superAdminTenantGuard, userAppGuard, tenantUserGuard, loginRedirectGuard.
  • State: 18 signal stores (signalStore), a central AuthStore; HTTP through Angular HttpClient and five functional interceptors (API prefix, credentials plus CSRF, encryption, error with refresh, loading).
  • Auth client: APP_INITIALIZER restores the session; CryptoSessionService performs the handshake; the session lives in HttpOnly cookies, not in localStorage; 15-minute inactivity logout. Requests: see the backend Auth flow table.

Test ID strategy

Verdict: there is no test-ID strategy. Counts over FE/src (160 TypeScript files, 59 components with inline templates, 1 HTML file that is index.html):

Selector hookOccurrences
data-testid, data-test, data-cy, data-qa0
Static id="..." and [id] bindings0
aria-label (one dynamic [attr.aria-label])1
role=11
formControlName (stable field names such as username, password)96
placeholder=81
Taiga attribute directives: tuiButton 37, tuiTab 13, tuiLabel 4; element <tui-...> 458
name="..." (144, mostly Lucide icon names such as trash-2, pencil)icon names, not form hooks

Consequence for automation: locate by role plus accessible name or visible text (Spanish UI strings), by formControlName attribute for form fields, and by Taiga directive attributes; expect instability when copy changes. The right fix is on the development side: add data-testid to actionable elements, starting with login, the tenant list and the CRUD dialogs. The login form is the first target for /test-framework-adaptation.

Monitoring and observability

Serilog to console, file and MongoDB; business-operation logs in MongoDB, readable from the admin screens; one health endpoint (/api/health, four checks, also used by the Compose healthcheck). No error tracker, uptime monitor, APM, metrics or alerting is configured in the repositories. Detail: nfr-observability.

Rollback

No rollback procedure is documented. In Compose the practical route is to check out the previous revision of both repositories and run docker compose up -d --build again; images are not tagged or pushed, so there is no previous image to redeploy. Pending migrations are applied forward automatically at API start, so a rollback of the code does not roll back the database; undoing a migration is a manual EF operation. For production the rollback tool (kubectl rollout undo or another) is the client's and unknown.

QA relevance

  • Test against the local Compose stack at https://localhost:18443: it is the only reachable environment and it runs outside Production mode, so plaintext fallbacks differ from the client's environment.
  • The certificate is local; use an option that ignores HTTPS errors in the browser and HTTP client.
  • The stack takes up to a minute to turn healthy (backend start period 30 seconds, depends on four healthy stores).
  • Reset data with docker compose down -v only on a local stack; it removes every volume.

CI/CD

Verdict: no pipeline exists in either repository. Checked on the tracked files of both repositories (branch sbx): no azure-pipelines*.yml, .azuredevops/, pipelines/, .github/, .gitlab-ci.yml, Jenkinsfile, .circleci/, vercel.json or netlify.toml. The only tracked YAML is BE/docker-compose.yml. The remotes are Azure DevOps, so a pipeline, if any, would live in Azure Pipelines outside the repositories (not visible).

QA relevance

With no pipeline there is no gate on merge and no scheduled run: when /regression-testing needs CI, the pipeline must be created first (Azure Pipelines is the natural host given the remotes), restoring the compose stack, then running the Playwright projects against it. That is a decision for the team, not something this phase assumes.

Discovery gaps

  • Kubernetes manifests missing. Production is described in BE/docs/Despliegue.md only; replica count, sticky sessions, probes, Ingress and secret handling are unverified. Needed to confirm NFR-SCAL-001.
  • Forwarded headers. No forwarded-headers handling was found in the API, while rate limiting and failed-login blocking key on the connection address. Behind nginx or an Ingress that address may be the proxy's, which would make the limits shared by all users. Verify on the running stack.
  • Redis fill side. The code that creates the tenant cache entries is not in these repositories, so cache lifetime and hit behaviour are unknown (NFR-PERF-002).
  • No performance target. No response-time goal, load test, query budget or connection-pool setting was found; no number is claimed.
  • SQL Server path not verified. The provider switch exists but only PostgreSQL was seen running; whether the single migration set supports SQL Server is unknown.
  • Secret location. The Phase 1 assessment records BE/MultitenantValidate.API/appsettings.json as git-ignored and not committed. The tracked Compose file has a default database credential fallback; confirm it is restricted to local development and never reused.
  • Unopened files. BE/.env and the Postman environment under BE/tests/postman/ were not opened by policy; their content and whether they hold credentials are unknown.
  • Compliance. Colombian data-protection obligations (consent, retention, data-subject requests) are not evidenced in code or docs; the product owner must state which apply.
  • Observability outside the app. No alerting, metrics or tracing evidence; client-side tooling, if any, is not visible from the repositories.
  • Non-Production environment used for evidence. The live Swagger and health endpoint were read from the local Compose stack (HTTPS port 18443), which is not running in Production mode; behaviours marked as Production-only were read from code, not observed.
  • Tests and CI. Neither repository has automated tests or pipelines; Phase 3 records the CI/CD finding.
  • Figure scope. The architecture figure shows containers only; the biometric components, the national-registry operators and the ATDP worker's consumer are outside these repositories and are not drawn.
  • Local-only configuration file. BE/MultitenantValidate.API/appsettings.json is git-ignored, has no template in the repository, and Program.cs requires it (optional: false). A fresh clone therefore cannot start the API on the host, and the Compose image only builds when the file exists in the build context. Needed: a committed example file or a documented list of required keys.
  • Test-ID strategy. The front end has no data-testid, no id and one aria-label; selectors must rely on roles, visible Spanish text and formControlName. Finding for the development team.
  • No automated tests and no pipeline. No test project in the backend, 0 spec files in the front end (npm test runs Vitest over nothing), and no pipeline files in either repository. Azure Pipelines definitions, if any, are outside the repositories and not visible.
  • Compose variable drift. LogQuery__MaxDateRangeDays is in BE/.env.example but not forwarded by compose, so setting it in .env has no effect in containers. ATDP_WORKER_URL is read by compose but missing from .env.example, and its default http://localhost:9091 points to the container itself.
  • Framework configuration is partially unset. .agents/project.yaml has webapp_domain, database.db_type and the QA, staging and production web/API URLs set to null. The local URLs and testing.default_env=local match the Compose target. Confirm the database value, domain and any external environment URLs with the team; see environments.
  • Production and QA addresses unknown. No QA or production URL, branch mapping, approval step, registry, backup policy or rollback procedure is documented; the client owns them.
  • Front-end bundle size and browser targets. The initial-bundle budget is declared (1.1 MB warning, 1.2 MB error) but the actual size was not measured, and no browser list is declared.
  • Production environment name on the local stack. The value of ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT in BE/.env was not opened; the non-Production mode is inferred from the exposed Swagger.
  • Machine-login payload. How the data field of POST /api/auth/login/api is encoded was not read (see BE/tests/postman/generate-api-login-payload.js).
  • Deployment figure. No separate topology figure: the architecture figure already shows the containers and the tables here carry the matrices.
